name: Psyllium (a fibre supplement)
summary: Psyllium is the husk of the seeds of a plant called Plantago ovata, also known as ispaghula. It is a mostly soluble fibre: with water it swells into a thick gel, and it passes through the gut largely undigested and not broken down by gut bacteria. It is sold as husk, powder or capsules, and is used for constipation and to lower cholesterol.
roles: Holds water in the bowel, making stools softer and bulkier
Forms a gel in the small intestine that slows how fast food is digested and absorbed
Lowers LDL cholesterol (the 'bad' cholesterol) in trials
Counts towards dietary fibre intake, which EFSA links to normal bowel function

status.note: There is no blood test for fibre intake or 'fibre status'. Intake is judged from what a person eats, against EFSA's adequate intake for dietary fibre of 25 g a day for adults (EFSA is the European Food Safety Authority). The markers in this app that psyllium trials measured are LDL cholesterol, fasting glucose and HbA1c (average blood sugar over about 3 months); they show the effect of everything a person eats and does, not fibre intake itself.

signs: Hard or infrequent stools (constipation): EFSA based its adequate intake for fibre on normal bowel function
There is no deficiency disease from too little fibre, and no test shows a shortage
atRisk: People who eat few whole grains, pulses, fruit, vegetables and potatoes, the main sources of fibre
Many adults in Europe: EFSA found average intakes of 16 to 29 g a day, often below the 25 g adequate intake

signs: Gas (flatulence) and bloating, more common with fibre than with placebo in trials
Blockage of the gullet or bowel, rare, when psyllium is swallowed without enough fluid or by people with swallowing problems or a narrowed gut
Allergic reactions, rare, mostly in people who have handled psyllium powder at work
high.note: EFSA set no upper limit for dietary fibre. The problems with psyllium come from how it is used rather than from a set amount: it swells with water, so too little fluid can let it form a lump that blocks the gullet or bowel. Case reports describe this in an older man with Parkinson's disease, a young man with constipation who drank too little, and after a gastric band operation. Gas and bloating are common at first.

examples: Psyllium is not an everyday food; it is added to some breakfast cereals
Fibre in general: whole grain cereals, pulses (beans, lentils, chickpeas), fruit, vegetables and potatoes
Gel-forming soluble fibre like psyllium's: beta-glucan in oats and barley
foodSources.note: The food table's fibre values are total fibre. They do not say how much of it is gel-forming, which is what lowers cholesterol and blood sugar in trials; fibres that don't form a gel (such as inulin or wheat bran) do not have those effects.

forms.name: Psyllium husk (whole flakes)
forms.note: The seed husk as it is. It is stirred into water or another drink and swallowed before it thickens. Trials of cholesterol, constipation and IBS used around 10 g a day (a median of 10.2 g in the cholesterol trials), as research, not as a dose for anyone.

forms.name: Psyllium powder (ground husk)
forms.note: Ground husk. It needs the same plenty of fluid: one case of a blocked gullet followed psyllium husk powder. Breathing in the powder is how people who handle it at work became allergic.

forms.name: Capsules
forms.note: Contain powdered husk, which swells in the same way, so fluid matters with capsules too.

forms.name: Psyllium-enriched foods
forms.note: Some breakfast cereals have psyllium added. A 1997 meta-analysis found that psyllium-enriched cereals lowered total and LDL cholesterol in adults with high cholesterol.

reference.noUpperLimit: EFSA set no tolerable upper intake level for dietary fibre. Its 2010 opinion set an adequate intake of 25 g a day for adults, based on normal bowel function, and noted that diets rich in fibre-containing foods with more than 25 g a day were linked to lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes and better weight maintenance. The 25 g is for fibre from all foods; it is not an amount of psyllium. The risks of psyllium itself (blockage when taken with too little fluid, allergy) don't depend on a fixed amount.

interactions.note: In trials psyllium lowered blood sugar most in people being treated for type 2 diabetes, and its researchers said more studies are needed on using it with glucose-lowering medicines. Blood sugar could fall further than expected. Talk to your doctor before adding it.

interactions.with: Other medicines taken at the same time
interactions.note: The gel can change how much of a medicine is absorbed and how fast. A 2012 review found few clinical studies, with variable results, and both helpful and harmful effects possible. Psyllium is often advised to be taken apart from other medicines; a pharmacist can say how far apart for a given medicine.
A 1990 case report described an interaction between lithium and ispaghula husk. Lithium needs steady blood levels, so this is one to discuss with the doctor or pharmacist.
In 3 trials, adding psyllium to a statin lowered LDL cholesterol further. That is a reason to tell the doctor, not to change a statin.

cautions: Psyllium swells with water. Swallowed with too little fluid, it has blocked the gullet or bowel in case reports, which is why it is meant to be mixed with plenty of fluid.
Not suitable without a doctor's advice for people with swallowing difficulties, a narrowed or blocked bowel, or after stomach operations such as a gastric band.
Gas and bloating are common, especially at first.

People who handle psyllium powder at work (nurses, pharmaceutical workers) can become allergic; in one study of hospital staff 5 to 12 % were sensitised, and rare cases of asthma and anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction) have followed.
Constipation that is new, lasts, or comes with blood, weight loss or pain is a reason to see a doctor rather than to use a laxative.
Some of the most positive analyses (blood sugar, weight, statins) were written by staff of a company that sells psyllium.

commonUses: May help lower cholesterol, especially LDL (the cholesterol that builds up in artery walls).
May help keep blood sugar steadier, mainly in people with type 2 diabetes.
May support regular bowel movements and ease constipation.
May help people feel full for longer after eating.

origin: Psyllium is the husk of the seeds of Plantago ovata, a plant also called ispaghula that is grown mainly in India. It is a mostly soluble fibre: with water it swells into a thick gel and passes through the gut largely undigested.
Supplements are made by milling the seeds to separate the husk, which is then sold whole as husk flakes, ground into powder, or put into capsules. Some breakfast cereals also have psyllium added.
dosage: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) sets an adequate intake (AI) of 25 g a day of dietary fibre for adults, based on normal bowel function. This is for fibre from all foods, not an amount of psyllium. EFSA set no tolerable upper intake level for fibre. These are population values, not personal targets.

An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is about 10 g of psyllium husk a day (a median of about 10 g in the cholesterol trials). This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

When checking a label, look at whether the product is husk, powder or capsules, and how much psyllium husk is in one serving. Psyllium swells with water and has blocked the gullet or bowel when swallowed with too little fluid, so it is meant to be mixed with plenty of fluid. Gas and bloating are common at first. It can change how much of other medicines is absorbed and may lower blood sugar further in people on diabetes medicines, so a doctor or pharmacist should be asked. Not suitable without a doctor's advice for people with swallowing difficulties or a narrowed or blocked bowel.

targets.label: EFSA adequate intake, total dietary fibre, adults
Psyllium husk commonly used in studies

foodAmounts.verdict: Partly. The total fibre intake of adults can be reached from ordinary food such as whole grains, pulses, fruit and vegetables. Psyllium itself is not an everyday food, and the food table lists total fibre without showing how much of it forms a gel, which is what the studies of cholesterol and blood sugar tested, so the amounts used in studies are not directly comparable with foods.
foodAmounts.notChecked: The food table gives total fibre only. Oats and barley contain a different gel-forming fibre, beta-glucan, which has been studied for cholesterol separately from psyllium.
